vignette:
Joseph has worked in the plumbing and electrical aisle of a big-box home improvement store for the past fifteen years. He always took pride in his work, in the quiet authority of knowing exactly which fitting a customer needed to fix a leaky faucet or which gauge of wire was right for a new ceiling fan. He was the man people sought out for solutions. For most of his 65 years, Joseph saw the world as a series of problems that, with the right tools and enough patience, could be fixed.

That sense of order shattered two years ago, the night the hurricane came. He and his wife, Adeola, had lived in their small brick home for over thirty years. It was the first and only home they bought after immigrating from Nigeria, the place where they had raised their children and planted a garden of collard greens and tomatoes every spring. They had weathered storms before. But this one was different.

He remembers the sound first—a low, guttural roar that wasn't just wind. He went to the basement to check the sump pump and saw the water seeping, then pouring, through the window wells. Within minutes, it was ankle-deep. He remembers Adeola calling his name from the top of the stairs, her voice tight with a fear he had never heard before. The lights flickered and died. The last thing he saw in the beam of his flashlight was his father’s old trunk, a precious link to his past, beginning to float in the murky water before the basement door slammed shut from the pressure. The sound of the wood splintering as the water forced its way upstairs is a sound that has never left him. They spent the rest of the night on the second floor, listening to their life being destroyed below them.

They live in an apartment now, on the third floor. Joseph insisted on it; he needed to be high up. But he hasn't escaped the water. Any heavy rain sends a jolt of ice through his veins. He keeps the weather app open on his phone constantly, his thumb scrolling through radar maps with an obsessive rhythm. He’ll stand at the window for hours, watching the clouds gather, his shoulders hiked up to his ears. Adeola will gently touch his arm and say, “It’s just a storm, my love,” but he can’t hear her. He’s listening for that roar, for the groan of a house giving way.

Sleep offers little respite. He often wakes up gasping, the phantom sensation of cold, dirty water closing over him. More often than not, he ends up on the couch, unwilling to disturb Adeola with his thrashing. In the quiet of the living room, his mind replays the event on a loop, but with new, torturous endings. He sees himself reinforcing the windows, building a higher retaining wall, convincing Adeola to leave days earlier. Each imagined success is just another reminder of his failure to protect them.

At work, the man who once solved problems now avoids them. When a customer asks about sump pumps, a wave of nausea hits him, and he has to walk away, pretending to check inventory. The smell of damp soil and fertilizer in the garden center can make him feel dizzy and disoriented, as if the floodwaters are rising around him right there in the aisle. He is often irritable, snapping at coworkers or customers over trivial matters, a stark contrast to the patient, calm man he used to be. He feels a profound sense of detachment from everything. The laughter of his colleagues in the breakroom sounds distant, like it’s coming from another world. He just watches, feeling like a ghost haunting the edges of his own life, a man who knows all the right parts but can no longer figure out how to fix himself.
